doc.title: Eddie Marshall interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: The Fourth Way, Santana and the Keystone
summary: Mike Nock and Michael White drew him to San Francisco for the Fourth Way, which opened at the Fillmore and toured with Santana; later he was in the Keystone house trio.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Okay. Because we kind of skipped over — I wanted to talk about the Fourth Way.

Oh boy. Well that’s another reason I stayed on the West Coast so long. Because actually after I came out here with Dionne and everything and I was in L.A. — L.A. I couldn’t really hang because L.A. is more like a recording industry and I’ve always played live music. So we were going to leave L.A. actually and go back to New York, when the baby was like a few months old. But Mike Nock, who was the piano player with Dionne, he had moved out to the West Coast. He had left Dionne’s band before I did. And he went to the West Coast, he ended up in San Francisco and worked with John Handy. And all this was going — there was a West Coast scene going on, but I didn’t know it, I’m back — and he says well before you go back, I’m going to start a band, me and Michael White are going to start this band, just come up and see if you want to deal with it. You can stay at Michael White’s house, you don’t have to pay rent and stuff. So we drove up here, and Michael White was living in Oakland, and we start, this was the Fourth Way. Well I started really enjoying living in San Francisco because I had never played any really like rock & roll type music, I’d played R&B but this was more like rock and jazz. And I remember I was still smoking cigarettes and I remember like the first week or so, you’re just playing really hard all the time and I’m going [pants] and I quit smoking, I quit this twenty year smoking habit, because I was just getting pooped. And the band actually took off and we played a lot of clubs here and oh the guy Bill Graham, that whole scene was starting, and he sort of liked that band. And we got hired to play a lot of opening acts at the Fillmore. We’d open for the Grateful Dead, we’d open for Miles one time, we opened for — a whole lot of different bands. But the one that was most important, we opened for Santana. And Santana really liked us so he took us on tour with him, I mean we went to Europe to the Montreux Jazz Festival with Santana, and I’ve always respected that guy since forever, because he always gives like jazz players a break to make money you know what I mean? He thinks that we ain’t making anything, so, even to this day he still does stuff like that. And so the band took off, and that lasted like three or four years, and living in the Bay Area and I just sort of got used to living here, then I’m working out of here every now and then, and then I still thought I might go back, because you always get that feeling you know. Because my family’s back east and everything. Then the Keystone Club opened, the Keystone opened up. And so I’m working there, me and James Berry and basically it was the rhythm section from Bobby Hutcherson’s band. I started working with Bobby around that time also. And we worked at the Keystone, we were like the house band, George Cables and I forget the bass player’s name already, anyhow we were like a house trio there. And there was no reason to leave then because all the guys that I would be working for in New York, they were all coming here. And so James Leary was the bass player. And so that lasted for five years. By that time I was too old to go back.
You’d established yourself in the area.
